denominator.verdict: No authoritative source enumerates which central banks use external reserve managers, and the body best placed to publish such a list states in terms that it does not. The row can therefore have an ESTIMATED POPULATION denominator but never a roster denominator. The recommended honest denominator is: 80 places filed against an estimated ~140-148 central banks that use external managers, i.e. about 54-57% — derived from the World Bank RAMP biennial survey finding that almost three-quarters of central bank respondents use external managers. The present '41% of 192 places' should be retired: 192 is the count of all places on the map, and roughly a quarter of central banks do not use an external manager at all, so 192 cannot be the denominator of this row.

why_no_roster_exists.point: The only global census of reserve management practice is anonymised by design.
why_no_roster_exists.quote: Survey results are presented in an aggregate format to preserve anonymity.
why_no_roster_exists.source: World Bank Treasury RAMP, Reserve Management Survey Report 2025 (5th edition), Introduction, p.13
why_no_roster_exists.note: The identical sentence appears in the 2023 (4th edition) report's Appendix, 'Survey Background and Methodology'. Both were read from the publisher's own PDF/text layer, not from a fetch summary.

why_no_roster_exists.point: The surveyor also measures, and reports as low, the public disclosure that a roster would have to be built from.
why_no_roster_exists.quote: Fewer than a quarter of central banks disclosed their investment policies, guidelines, risk metrics, or characteristics of external management programs.
why_no_roster_exists.source: World Bank Treasury RAMP, Reserve Management Survey Report 2023 (4th edition), Governance chapter, p.13 (Figure 12: Information disclosed to the public, either on a mandatory or a voluntary basis)

why_no_roster_exists.point: The inaugural edition said the same about external managers specifically, in its list of key findings on reporting and transparency.
why_no_roster_exists.quote: A majority of institutions do not provide information on institutional regulation, risk metrics, benchmarks, external managers and investment horizon.
why_no_roster_exists.source: Inaugural RAMP Survey on the Reserve Management Practices of Central Banks: Results and Observations (2019), key findings, p.11

why_no_roster_exists.point: The 2025 edition confirms disclosure has not improved.
why_no_roster_exists.quote: The level of disclosure to the public about foreign reserves has not changed significantly as compared to previous surveys and remains overall limited
why_no_roster_exists.source: Reserve Management Survey Report 2025, 'Disclosure to the public' (Figure 14, N: 133)

denominator.recommended_chart_wording: 80 of an estimated ~145 central banks that use an external manager (World Bank RAMP 2025: almost three-quarters of 136 respondents use external managers). No list of which central banks use external managers is published by anyone; the RAMP survey, the only global census, is anonymised by design and reports that fewer than a quarter of central banks disclose anything about their external management programmes.
denominator.second_ceiling_worth_showing: There is a separate and much lower ceiling on what this row can ever document from the CENTRAL BANK's own side: fewer than a quarter of central banks disclose the characteristics of their external management programmes (RAMP 2023), i.e. under about 48 of 192. The row already stands at 80 places because most of it rests on the MANAGER's disclosure rather than the bank's — NBIM's own published mandate list, World Bank RAMP press releases and member statements, and three currency-union financial statements (BCEAO, BEAC, ECCB) that expand to many member countries from one document. That is worth saying on the chart, because it explains how the row can exceed the central banks' own disclosure rate and warns that the remaining places are mostly ones where no document will ever name a manager.

what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.source: World Bank Treasury RAMP — Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership. RAMP is itself an external manager and advisor and so would be the single largest nameable block.
what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.result: The public 'Global Network' page at treasury.worldbank.org no longer carries a member list; it was fetched and reads as events and programme description only (9,591 characters of text after tag-stripping, no country or member names). The only published aggregate found is RAMP's own 2024 one-pager: 'Today, RAMP members also include international financial institutions, public pension funds, and sovereign wealth funds, with over 70 members worldwide' — which bounds the RAMP vein at under 70 central banks and does not name them.

what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.source: World Bank RAMP biennial Reserve Management Survey, all five editions (2019 inaugural, 2021 3rd, 2023 4th, 2025 5th). All four obtainable PDFs/text layers downloaded and grepped in full for 'external manager', 'externally managed', 'external management'.
what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.result: Gives the PROPORTION in every edition and never a country. Explicitly anonymised (quoted above). This is the authoritative periodic survey of reserve management practice that the assignment asked for, and it is the reason a roster cannot exist.

what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.source: IMF, Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Reserve Management (2001/2004) and its Accompanying Document and Case Studies (2003).
what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.result: NOT REACHED as a document this round — identified by search only (imf.org/external/pubs/ft/ferm/guidelines/2005/index.htm and the Accompanying Document and Case Studies manual page). Flagged as a lead rather than a check: the Accompanying Document is a volume of voluntary country case studies, so it names at most the twenty-odd countries that chose to contribute, is from 2003, and would be a source of RECORDS rather than of a denominator. It cannot supply an enumeration because participation in it was voluntary.

what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.source: BIS — Markets Committee and BIS Papers, searched for a periodic survey of reserve management practice.
what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.result: NOT REACHED as a document. The search returned only BIS Papers 40 and a 2006 BIS Quarterly Review article as candidates, neither confirmed to carry a survey of external manager use, and the trade-press 'Trends in reserve management' series. No BIS equivalent of the RAMP survey was identified. Recorded as not reached, not as a confirmed absence.

what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.source: Central Banking Publications' annual 'Trends in reserve management' survey (the HSBC/Central Banking series), 2018 through 2026 editions.
what_was_checked_and_found_no_roster.result: NOT OPENED. Located by search but not fetched: it is trade press behind a paywall, so under the project's rules any figure from it is weak_source, and the RAMP series already supplies the same quantity from a primary publisher with a stated sample. Left as a lead for cross-checking only.

task3_norway_concentration.finding: Norway is just under half the row's ties and nearly three-quarters of its distinct party names, and every one of those ties comes from a single web page. The row's TIE count is not comparable with any other row on the map and the chart should count PLACES.
two_further_problems_with_the_norway_blo: It is not foreign exchange reserves. The filed detail says so itself: the 103 firms are listed by Norges Bank Investment Management as external managers of the Government Pension Fund Global, a sovereign wealth fund that Norges Bank manages on the finance ministry's behalf. Every other large block on the row (RAMP, the BIS, Amundi, Crown Agents, BlackRock) is about FX reserves or a lending programme. Counting them together makes one country's wealth-fund manager roster look like a measure of reserve outsourcing.

It is a disclosure artefact, not a difference in behaviour. Norway appears 103 times because NBIM publishes its full mandate list; a central bank with the same number of managers that publishes nothing appears zero times. So the tie count measures transparency, not outsourcing, and the RAMP finding that fewer than a quarter of central banks disclose their external management programmes is the direct evidence for that.
task3_norway_concentration.recommendation: Count places, not ties, for this row's completeness figure, and if a tie count is shown anywhere, show it as '233 ties, of which 103 are one fund's published manager list'. Consider whether the Norway block belongs on this relation at all or on a separate wealth-fund relation.

blanks.note: Bank of Mauritius Annual Report 2024 (bom_ar_2024_final.pdf, 480,843 characters) could not be downloaded for grepping: www.bom.mu and bom.mu both fail TLS verification here ('unable to get local issuer certificate'), under a bare curl, with --cacert /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt, and with --proxy-cacert as well, so this is the host's own certificate chain and not the agent proxy, whose status reports bundleCoversEveryHost true. The 2025 report (bom_ar_2025_web.pdf) fails the same way. A WebFetch of the 2024 report returned only the first 100,000 characters, covering up to Chapter 4, and found no firm named; the reserve management discussion and the financial statement notes were NOT reached. The country has not been tested. The 2018 annual report (annual_report_june_2018.pdf) was returned by search for the phrase 'external fund managers' and is the better document to try next, through WebFetch with offsets.

Central Bank of Iceland: cb.is/markets-and-market-operations/international-reserves/ returns HTTP 200 at 3,853 bytes, which is a JavaScript shell with no reserve text in the HTML; cb.is/about-the-bank/international-reserves returns 404 at 3,955 bytes. The website route is closed for this country. The annual reports are mirrored as PDFs on rafhladan.is (Annual Report 2011, 2012 and a combined AR_Heildarskjal file came back in search) and are the route to try; none was opened this round, so the country is untested on the document side.

Refused on a wrong-document check rather than filed. The URL vpr.hkma.gov.hk/statics/assets/doc/400754/ar_24/ar_24_eng.pdf was returned by search as an HKMA annual report and downloads cleanly (7,004,624 bytes, 660,539 characters of text), but the document is a Mauritian commercial bank's annual report: it names EY Mauritius and KPMG as external auditors, refers to the Bank of Mauritius as its regulator and to MUA Pension Ltd and Orange Eight Ltd for its staff pension scheme. Nothing about Hong Kong or the Exchange Fund. A quiet wrong document behind an hkma.gov.hk hostname — worth recording so the next round does not spend a call on it. HKMA's own annual report and Exchange Fund disclosures remain unopened.

Row-wide: the RAMP membership route, which produced a large share of what is already filed, is closed on the manager's side. The World Bank Treasury 'Global Network' page no longer publishes a member list, and the RAMP 2024 one-pager gives only an aggregate ('over 70 members worldwide', central banks plus IFIs, pension funds and sovereign wealth funds). New RAMP ties will now have to come one at a time from World Bank press releases on individual joinings, or from the member central bank's own report. A search for '"joins World Bank" RAMP' returned only the Bosnia and Herzegovina joining, which is already filed (BIH), and the Turkic Investment Fund, which is not a central bank.

checked_not_in_assignment: NOR, COL, KAZ, TLS, CHL, EST, GTM, BOL, BIH, ARM, BGR — all read out of have_mgr.json before any searching, and all already on the row. No country was added from prose.
MUS, ISL, HKG — each confirmed present in absent.json under reserve_managers before being worked on.
leads_not_opened: Bank of Mauritius Annual Report June 2018, https://www.bom.mu/sites/default/files/annual_report_june_2018.pdf — returned by a search for the exact phrase 'external fund managers' alongside the Bank of Mauritius. bom.mu fails TLS here, so it must be read through WebFetch with offsets, or through a mirror. Highest-probability single record left from this round's searching.

Central Bank of Iceland annual reports mirrored on rafhladan.is (e.g. https://rafhladan.is/bitstream/handle/10802/13178/Annual%20Report%202012.pdf?sequence=8 and the combined https://rafhladan.is/bitstream/handle/10802/13178/AR_Heildarskjal%20N%c3%bdtt.pdf?sequence=9). The mirror is a plain file host, so curl plus grep should work where cb.is does not.

IMF, Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Reserve Management: Accompanying Document and Case Studies (2003), https://www.imf.org/en/publications/manuals-guides/issues/2016/12/30/guidelines-for-foreign-exchange-reserve-management-accompanying-document-and-case-studies-17343 — a volume of voluntary country case studies. Not a denominator, but about twenty countries describing their own reserve management in their own words, which is exactly the kind of document that names a manager. Old (2003), so any record off it needs an as_of of 2003 and should be read as historic.

Central Banking Publications, 'Trends in reserve management 2026: survey results', https://www.centralbanking.com/central-banks/reserves/7975827/trends-in-reserve-management-2026-survey-results — paywalled trade press, so weak_source if used, but it is the only annual series independent of RAMP and would cross-check the three-quarters figure against a different respondent sample.

BIS Papers 40, https://www.bis.org/publ/bppdf/bispap40.pdf, and the BIS Quarterly Review article at https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt0609e.pdf — the two BIS candidates a search surfaced for a survey of reserve management practice. Neither opened. If a BIS Markets Committee survey of external manager use exists, it is the one remaining chance at a second independent aggregate.

The row's own three union documents (BCEAO and BEAC financial statements, ECCB annual report) are already filed and expand to many member countries. No comparable multi-country single document was found for any other region, but the CEMAC/BEAC and ECCB pattern suggests checking whether any other shared institution — the Eastern Caribbean, CFA franc zone aside — publishes a single statement covering several central banks.
